messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Minh Tran was 35 when he became seriously ill, a married Vietnamese American man who had always thought of himself as dependable, careful, and productive. He worked as a UX designer for a tech company, spending most days at a screen mapping user flows, joining video calls, and keeping track of timelines and revisions. The illness began in a way that still felt frighteningly ordinary to him: a period of feeling unwell that stretched on longer than it should have, followed by a rapid escalation that ended in emergency care. What stayed with Minh was not a single dramatic image so much as the lived sense that his body had become dangerous territory without warning. He remembered waiting for updates, for test results, for someone to explain why things were taking so long, and with each delay becoming more certain that something catastrophic was unfolding just out of view. By the time the danger had passed, he no longer experienced waiting as neutral. Any delay had come to feel like the beginning of terrible news.

In the months afterward, Minh did what he could to put the whole episode behind him. He did not want to think about the illness, the hospital, the uncertainty, or the helplessness of being told to wait. If his wife tried to bring up how frightening that period had been, he would go quiet or change the subject. He told himself there was no point dwelling on it, but privately he also felt unable to tolerate what came up when he let his mind drift there. He avoided hospitals whenever possible, looked away when ambulances passed in traffic, and postponed routine physical examinations. Even seeing a medical building from the car window could make his body tighten before he had consciously registered why. He described himself as being tense all the time, shoulders raised, stomach clenched, as if he were bracing for something to go wrong again.

That vigilance began to spread into ordinary parts of his life. At work, if a teammate took too long to reply on Slack, if a product review meeting ran over, or if a loading screen stalled during testing, Minh felt a jolt of alarm that far exceeded the moment. The felt logic was immediate: when things take longer than expected, something bad is happening. He knew other people did not react this way, and he could hear how disproportionate it sounded when he tried to explain it, but reassurance did not land. Even when his wife told him he was fine, or a doctor’s office later confirmed that a delay was just administrative, he found it impossible to feel safe. His mind did not settle with information; his body remained keyed up, prepared for danger.

He also started avoiding anything that made his body feel strained. He stopped exercising in the ways he once had, and he became wary of exertion, heat, rushing, or anything that made his heart pound or his breathing change. The sensations themselves felt loaded now, too close to the bodily vulnerability he had discovered during the illness. He planned his days to minimize physical stress and became more rigid about conserving energy. This narrowed his life in ways that were hard to admit. He was less spontaneous with his wife, less willing to go out if it meant walking far or being away from home too long, and more likely to stay in controlled environments where he felt he could monitor himself.

Alongside this, Minh’s view of himself had changed in a painful way. He had come to believe there was something wrong with him as a person, not just with his body. Surviving the illness had not left him feeling fortunate or resilient; instead, he felt defective and weak. He compared himself unfavorably to other people who seemed able to handle medical uncertainty or bodily discomfort without falling apart inside. What troubled him most was how emotionally flat he had become. He described feeling dead inside, as though the version of him that used to enjoy things, engage easily, and feel present with his wife had receded. He still went through the motions of work and marriage, but much of it felt mechanical.

By the time he sought help, the strain was showing in concrete ways. He had delayed another physical examination despite knowing it was overdue, and the anticipation alone was affecting his sleep and concentration. At work he was finding it harder to manage routine project uncertainty because every unanswered message and every delayed decision stirred the same dread. His wife had begun to say that she missed him, that even when he was home he seemed far away. Minh came to treatment not because he felt hopeful, exactly, but because he was tired of living as if danger were always one step ahead. What frightened him most was the sense that he could never trust his own body or believe anyone who told him he was safe. What he wanted, quietly and with some shame, was to stop feeling so weak and to feel alive in his own life again.
